title: 2 Kings
subtitle: Melakhim Bet, “Kings”
description: The second half of the book of Kings, which carries the story of God’s people from the chariot of fire that took Elijah up to heaven to the burning of Jerusalem. Elisha takes up his master’s cloak: a widow’s oil flows until there are no more jars, a Shunammite’s son opens his eyes, Naaman washes seven times in the Jordan, and a frightened servant sees the hills full of horses and chariots of fire. Then the kingdoms fall, Samaria to Assyria and Jerusalem to Babylon, though not before Hezekiah spreads a threatening letter before the LORD and Josiah hears the book of the law and tears his clothes. It ends with a captive son of David released from prison to eat at the king’s table. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of 2 Kings?
qa.answer: The second half of the book of Kings in the Old Testament, which in Hebrew is a single book called Melakhim, “Kings”. Its twenty-five chapters run from the middle of the ninth century BC to about 561 BC. Chapters 1–8 tell of the prophet Elisha; chapters 9–17 follow the kingdoms of Israel and Judah to the fall of Samaria to Assyria in 722 BC; and chapters 18–25 follow Judah alone, through the reigns of Hezekiah, Manasseh and Josiah, to the destruction of Jerusalem by Babylon in 586 BC and the release of King Jehoiachin in exile.

qa.question: Who wrote 2 Kings, and when?
qa.answer: The book does not name its author. Jewish tradition, recorded in the Talmud, credited Kings to the prophet Jeremiah, and the last chapter of Jeremiah repeats the end of 2 Kings almost word for word. Many scholars think the book was completed during the exile in Babylon, since its last event, Jehoiachin’s release, can be dated to about 561 BC, and some think an earlier edition was made in the days of King Josiah. It draws on older royal records it names, the histories of the kings of Israel and of Judah.

qa.question: Why were Israel and Judah sent into exile?
qa.answer: 2 Kings answers the question directly in chapter 17, after the fall of Samaria: the people had worshipped other gods and refused to listen to the prophets the LORD sent them again and again, warning them to turn back. It says the same of Judah, especially after the long reign of Manasseh (21:10–15; 24:3–4). The book stresses that judgement came only after centuries of patience, and that even then God kept his promise to David alive in the person of the exiled king Jehoiachin.

qa.question: What is the story of Naaman in 2 Kings 5?
qa.answer: Naaman was commander of the army of Aram, an enemy of Israel, and he had a serious skin disease, traditionally called leprosy. On the advice of a captive Israelite girl he came to the prophet Elisha, who sent word that he should wash seven times in the Jordan. Naaman was offended by so plain a command, but his servants persuaded him, and he was made clean and confessed that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel. Jesus cited him in Luke 4:27 as one of the foreigners to whom God showed mercy.

qa.question: What happened to Elijah in 2 Kings 2?
qa.answer: As Elijah and his successor Elisha walked on together beyond the Jordan, a chariot of fire with horses of fire came between them, and Elijah went up to heaven in a whirlwind (2:11). Elijah did not die, which is one reason later Jewish hope expected his return before the day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5). Elisha, who had asked for a double portion of his spirit, took up the cloak Elijah left behind and struck the Jordan, and the water parted for him as it had for his master.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. “LORD” in capitals stands for God’s personal name. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Hebrew beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.
